86.title: Early Evolution of Religion
86.b0.ask: “Before revelation came, why and how did man come to have religion?”
86.b2.p: In Paper 85 we saw the origins of worship, when primitive man revered stones and trees, animals and the sky. Paper 86 now follows that urge to worship as it grows into religion. The evolution of religion described here does not depend on revelation. The normal working of the human mind, under the guidance of the sixth and seventh mind-adjutants, is wholly sufficient to bring it about.
86.b3.p: At first man simply feared the forces of nature. Then, as nature became personalized, spiritized, and finally deified in human consciousness, that fear gradually became religious. Chance and misfortune, unexplained death, and ancestors appearing in dreams were the steppingstones along the way.
86.b4.p: How, then, could this primitive religion, born of fear and full of mistaken ideas, prepare man for ethics and for genuine spiritual experience?
86.b7.h: 1. Chance: Good Luck and Bad Luck
86.b8.p: Besides the natural urge to worship, early religion was rooted in man’s experience of chance — good luck and bad luck. The results of hunting varied from day to day, and in a life lived on the ragged edge of existence, mischance was a great factor. Primitive man struggled for existence, not for a standard of living, and the constant dread of unseen calamity eclipsed every pleasure. A run of good luck was itself feared as a certain sign of coming disaster.
86.b9.p: Existence itself was a gamble. Primitive man swung between the passion of getting something for nothing and the fear of getting nothing for something. The later herders and farmers were no different: drought, floods, hail, pests — everything beyond their control was counted as good luck or bad luck.
86.b10.t: The ever-varying results of the hunt
The same views of chance and luck
Drought, floods, hail, storms, pests, plant diseases, heat and cold
86.b12.p: Primitive man constantly asked, “⟦Q 86:2.2⟧Who is tormenting me?⟦/Q⟧” Finding no material source for his miseries, he settled on a spirit explanation, and so religion was born of the fear of the mysterious and the awe of the unseen. His mind was logical but had few ideas to work with: if one event followed another, he took them to be cause and effect. And so nature and chance were personalized as ghosts and spirits, and later as gods.
86.b13.p: The book is sharp on this point. To keep ascribing things hard to understand to supernatural causes is a lazy and convenient way of avoiding intellectual hard work. But the exploration of life’s phenomena sooner or later destroys the belief in chance and puts in its place a universe of law and order in which every effect has a definite cause. Not all religions came from animism, however; other ideas of the supernatural also led to worship.
86.b16.p: Death was the supreme shock to evolving man, the most perplexing combination of chance and mystery. Not the sanctity of life but the shock of death inspired fear and so fostered religion. Among savages death usually came by violence, so a nonviolent death seemed all the more mysterious. The legends of men who did not die, found among all races, are traces of that early view of death as a kind of visitation.
86.b17.p: At first all disease and natural death were believed to come from spirit influence, and this idea lingered even in later theologies, giving rise to doctrines such as original sin and the fall of man. Realizing his helplessness before nature and his weakness before sickness and death, the savage placed their cause in a supermaterial world and turned to it for help.
86.b19.p: The idea that something survives death arose from the chance association of everyday events with the ghost dream. When several members of a tribe dreamed of their departed chief at the same time, it seemed proof that he had returned in some form. Breath, which looked like a cloud on a cold day, also fascinated early man; it marked the difference between the living and the dead. From the breath-dream idea came the most primitive concept of the human soul, the ghost. Breath without the body was a spirit, a ghost.
86.b20.p: This early belief in survival did not mean immortality. People who could not count over twenty could hardly grasp eternity, so they thought of recurring incarnations. The belief that man dies three to seven times is a remnant of Adam’s teachings about the mansion worlds. The future life was first pictured as just like this one, minus all ill luck; heaven and hell were conceived later. Each people had its own idea of the ghost soul’s destiny.
86.b21.t: The destiny of the ghost soul
Weak men have weak souls — Hades invented to receive them
Ghosts returned to the ancestral homelands
Soul and body remained together — careful tombs and preservation of the body
A phantom replica went down to Sheol and could not return
86.b23.p: The nonmaterial part of man has been called ghost, spirit, shade, phantom, specter, and later soul. To early man the soul was his dream double, exactly like himself except that it could not be touched. As civilization advances, this superstitious idea of the soul is destroyed, and man comes to understand the soul as the joint creation of the God-knowing mind and its indwelling divine spirit, the Thought Adjuster — a concept that depends on revelation and personal religious experience.
86.b24.p: The ancients believed the soul could leave the body in several ways, as perfume leaves a flower. Sneezing was taken as a failed attempt of the soul to escape, and so a blessing was spoken; sleepers were awakened gradually to give the soul time to return. Moses forbade the belief that God speaks in dreams, and the book says Moses was right, for spiritual personalities do not use ordinary dreams to communicate with material beings.
86.b25.t: Ways the soul leaves the body
86.b26.p: The soul was usually identified with the breath, but some peoples located it in the head, hair, heart, liver, blood, or fat. Breath, shadows, and reflections in water were all taken as evidence of the soul. Ideas about the number of souls varied as well.
86.b27.t: Two souls: the breath and the shadow
Vegetative soul (stomach), animal soul (heart), intellectual soul (head)
Three parts: body, soul, and name
86.b29.p: Man inherited a natural environment, acquired a social environment, and imagined a ghost environment, and institutions arose in response to each. The imagined spirit world was accepted as real very early, and it changed the mental and moral life of all mankind for all time.
86.b31.p: If angry ghosts send bad luck and pleased ones good fortune, then human conduct must be regulated accordingly. Here the concept of right and wrong was born — long before any revelation. There followed a long and wasteful struggle to appease ever-displeased spirits, yet it was worth all it cost, for in it human ethics was born. The book’s remark that each generation smiles at its ancestors’ superstitions while holding fallacies that posterity will smile at asks humility of us too.
86.b33.p: Primitive religion was insurance against the perils of the forest. The savage willingly paid heavy premiums of fear, superstition, and gifts to priests. Modern society has moved the business of insurance into the realm of economics, and religion is slowly rising from a scheme of insurance against bad luck to higher philosophic levels. Even so, the old religion kept men from becoming fatalistic and hopelessly pessimistic, because it made them believe they could do something to influence fate.
86.b34.t: How bad luck was guarded against
Premiums of fear, superstition, and gifts to priests
Material premiums against the accidents of industry and modern life
An actuary’s reckoning in place of whimsical gods
86.b35.p: The book adds a further warning. While men are giving up the idea that spirits cause life’s ups and downs, they readily accept an almost equally fallacious teaching that blames all human inequalities on political, social, and industrial causes. Only an understanding of facts and wise action within the laws of nature is the antidote for so-called accidental ills. And primitive religion, by the power of false fear, prepared the soil of the human mind for the bestowal of the Thought Adjuster.
86.b38.p: Paper 86 does not hide the fact that religion had humble beginnings. The luck of the hunt, unexplained death, ancestors in dreams, and breath like a cloud gave rise to a world of ghosts and spirits, and man spent vast effort over long ages trying to appease that imagined world. Yet in that very fear the sense of right and wrong grew and human ethics was born, and man held on to the hope that he could do something about his own destiny. Into the soil of the mind plowed by false fear came the Thought Adjuster, who is still at work turning the fear of God into the love of God.
86.b39.t: 1. Chance: Good Luck and Bad Luck
On the edge of survival, fear of chance became a root of religion
Suffering of unknown cause was personalized as ghosts, spirits, and gods
Not the sanctity of life but the shock of death fostered religion
Dreams and breath gave rise to ideas of survival and the ghost soul
The dream double was the beginning of the idea of the soul
Trying to appease an imagined spirit world gave birth to right and wrong
Religion as insurance against fear prepared the soil for the Adjuster
86.b41.box: Religion that began in fear gave birth to human ethics and prepared the mind for the Adjuster, and now that fear is being changed into the love of God.
87.title: The Ghost Cults
87.b0.ask: “How can rituals that grew out of fear of the dead become the skeleton of true religion?”
87.b2.p: In Paper 86 we saw how a world of ghosts and spirits was imagined out of chance and death, dreams and breath. Paper 87 now shows what man did about those imagined ghosts. The ghost cult arose as an offset to the hazards of bad luck, and its rites were mostly negative — designed to avoid, expel, or coerce ghosts. It was nothing more than insurance against disaster; it had nothing to do with investing in a higher future.
87.b3.p: Mankind has had a long and bitter struggle with the ghost cult, and nothing in human history excites more pity than man’s abject slavery to ghost-spirit fear. Yet that very fear set mankind on the upgrade of religious evolution. Human imagination cast off from the shores of self, and it will not find anchor again until it arrives at the concept of a true Deity, a real God.
87.b4.p: What, then, in these cults so full of fear, deception, and waste, should we carry forward today?
87.b8.p: Death was feared because it meant the release of another ghost from its body. A ghost was feared most during the transition between death and its departure for the ghost homeland. The savage credited ghosts with supernatural power but not supernatural intelligence, so he used every kind of trick to fool them. The book observes that civilized man still hopes an outward show of piety will somehow deceive even an omniscient Deity.
87.b9.p: A house where someone had died was destroyed or avoided, and this fear kept early man from building substantial houses and permanent villages. People sat up all night beside a corpse, fearing they too would die if they fell asleep near it, and they never left a dead body in the dark. There were many ways of deceiving the ghost.
87.b10.t: Removing the corpse through a hole in the wall
To confuse the ghost so it could not return
Returning from a funeral by a different road
So the ghost would not follow
So the ghost would not recognize the survivors
First a disguise; later a sign of respect to appease the ghost
87.b12.p: The negative program of placating ghosts came long before any positive program of coercing or entreating spirits. The first acts of human worship were acts of defense, not reverence. The funeral service grew out of the effort to send the ghost on to its future home, and the funeral sermon was first meant to teach the new ghost how to get there. It was believed to take from three days to a year to “⟦Q 87:2.3⟧lay the ghost.⟦/Q⟧”
87.b13.p: Mourning was a ritual of fear, not an expression of sorrow. Professional mourners were hired, and weeks and even months of each year were wasted in unproductive mourning. The names of the dead became taboo, and so languages were steadily impoverished. The book records plainly that because ghosts were thought to want wives and servants, people were buried alive or killed to accompany the dead. Tools and property were broken or burned to go with them, and it was a great advance in civilization when the inheritance of kin replaced this waste.
87.b14.t: Sending real objects and persons with the dead
Mourning out of respect and bereavement
87.b16.p: The advancing ghost cult made ancestor worship inevitable. It became the connecting link between common ghosts and the higher spirits, the evolving gods; the early gods were simply glorified departed humans. Even the custom of adopting children was meant to make sure someone would offer sacrifices for one’s soul after death.
87.b17.p: Most tribes held an all-souls’ feast at least once a year. The Romans had twelve ghost feasts a year, half the days of the year were given to ceremonies of this kind, and one emperor tried to reduce the feast days to 135 a year. As ghosts were imagined to pass on to higher stages of existence, the cult too progressed toward the worship of spirits and gods.
87.b19.p: For ages many tribes believed in one class of ghosts: when a ghost was pleased, there was good luck; when angered, bad luck. Then the concept of two kinds of spirits, good and bad, arose independently all over the world. This dualism let man account for both good and bad luck while believing in supermortal beings who were consistent in their behavior — one of the most momentous discoveries of truth in the history of religious evolution.
87.b20.t: One class of ghosts — good luck when pleased, bad luck when angered, wholly temperamental
Good spirits and bad spirits — each consistent in behavior
The idea of consistent supermortal forces
It became hard to conceive of cosmic unity
87.b21.p: But the price was terrible. The doctrine has ever since made it difficult for religionists to conceive of cosmic unity, and the gods of evolutionary religion have generally been set against the forces of darkness. The tragedy is that when this idea took root, there were no bad or disharmonious spirits in all the world. That situation did not develop until after the Caligastic rebellion, and it persisted only until Pentecost.
87.b23.p: Primitive man believed that spirits had almost unlimited rights but no duties, while man had many duties but no rights. After sacrificing to all known spirits, people did one more turn to the “unknown gods,” just to be safe. Religion was man’s adjustment to his illusions about the mystery of chance, and the worship of spirits was a prosperity insurance policy. Since good spirits were thought to go about their own business, people paid far more attention to the evil ones.
87.b24.p: Prosperity was believed to arouse the envy of evil spirits, and fear of the evil eye spread almost world-wide. So people learned to speak lightly of their success and to depreciate praise. Early humility was not a debasement of ego but an attempt to fool the envious spirits; in time it evolved into civilized modesty, restraint, and courtesy. On the other hand, the custom of looking ugly to avoid envy long held back the advance of art.
87.b25.t: What must be done to keep the spirits favorable, or at least neutral
The correct conduct and ceremonies to win the spirits to one’s interests
The correct understanding of spirits, and hence of life and death
87.b26.p: The will of the spirits was studied through omens, oracles, and signs, and interpreted by divination, soothsaying, magic, ordeals, and astrology. The ancients sought to know the future not out of curiosity but to dodge ill luck. Slow, very slow, is man to abandon the methods by which he has climbed so far.
87.b28.p: Once the idea of good and bad spirits arrived, rituals were no longer aimed only at warding off bad luck; they turned positive, seeking to win good luck. Before long man began to invent weapons with which to compel spirit co-operation. His first defenses were directed against ghosts, and many techniques arose to frighten them and drive them away.
87.b29.t: 1. Cutting off the head and tying up the body in the grave
To keep the ghost from leaving the grave
3. Castration or breaking the legs of the corpse
One origin of the modern tombstone
6. Casting the body into the sea
87.b30.p: Shouting, bells, drums, foul smells, and hideous images were used to drive ghosts off. Water was regarded as the best protection against ghosts; baptism and religious bathing came from this, and only recently has bathing become a sanitary practice. Exorcism was the use of one spirit to control or banish another, and primitive cursing was a means of overawing minor spirits. Vows, fasting, and self-denial were also believed to be sure ways of coercing spirits, and from this grew austerity. Modern man still swears, knocks on wood, and shows a disposition to bargain with Deity.
87.b32.p: The cult persisted because it provided a symbolism for preserving and stimulating moral sentiments and religious loyalties. Yet while the cult preserved sentiment, it has always been the greatest obstacle to social reconstruction and spiritual progress. A religious cult cannot be manufactured; it must grow. The early Christian cult was the most effective and enduring ritual ever devised, but in a scientific age it has been devitalized by the loss of many of its fundamental ideas.
87.b34.p: Every new revelation of truth has given rise to a new cult, and even the restatement of the religion of Jesus must develop a new symbolism — one predicated on the Fatherhood of God and pregnant with the ideal of the brotherhood of man. The old cults were too egocentric; the new must be the outgrowth of applied love.
87.b35.t: What the new cult must do
Foster sentiment, satisfy emotion, promote loyalty
Facilitate spiritual progress, enhance cosmic meanings, augment moral values, encourage social development
The biologic, sociologic, and religious significance of the home
Embody some mystery, and be meaningful to both the individual and the group
Becoming too complex or crystallizing into stifling stereotyped ceremonials
87.b37.p: Paper 87 shows without concealment the enormous effort and waste mankind spent deceiving, placating, and coercing ghosts. Fear of the dead held back houses and villages, impoverished language, and consumed property and time. Yet along the way the dualism of good and bad spirits gave rise to the truth of consistent supermortal forces, and the gestures meant to fool the spirits were refined into modesty and courtesy. In the end the paper says that the cult itself is not the problem. Rigid ritual blocks progress, but a living cult that grows out of applied love becomes the skeleton on which personal spiritual experience grows.
87.b38.t: Fearing the newly released ghost, men used every trick to deceive it
The first acts of human worship were defense, not reverence
The early gods were glorified departed humans
Dualism gave consistent spirits but obscured cosmic unity
Gestures to fool envious spirits grew into modesty and courtesy
Religion moved from placating spirits to trying to coerce them
A genuine cult grows, and the new cult must come from applied love
87.b40.box: The old cults born of fear are fading, and a new cult growing out of applied love, built on the Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, becomes the skeleton of true religion.
88.title: Fetishes, Charms, and Magic
88.b0.ask: “How did the fear of objects indwelt by spirits reach all the way to sacred books, national flags, and science?”
88.b2.p: In Paper 87 we saw the ghost cults, in which man tried to deceive, placate, and coerce ghosts. Paper 88 now moves on to the belief that spirits dwell in objects, animals, and people. The doctrine of spirit possession — a spirit entering an inanimate object, an animal, or a human being — is nothing more nor less than fetishism. The savage did not necessarily worship the fetish itself; quite logically, he worshiped the spirit he believed lived in it.
88.b3.p: At first the spirit of a fetish was believed to be the ghost of a dead man; later, higher spirits were thought to reside in fetishes. In this way the fetish cult gathered together all the primitive ideas of ghosts, souls, spirits, and demon possession.
88.b4.p: In what forms, then, does that old fear of pebbles and fingernail trimmings survive today? And how did it finally bear the fruit of science?
88.b8.p: Primitive man always wanted to make anything extraordinary into a fetish, and chance gave origin to many. Volcanoes, but not mountains, became fetishes; comets, but not stars. The first fetishes were peculiarly marked pebbles, and man has sought “sacred stones” ever since. Fire and water were also early fetishes, and fire worship and belief in holy water still survive.
88.b9.p: When a plant or animal became a fetish, eating it became taboo. Certain days and numbers were fetishes too. Parts of the body — saliva, hair, fingernails, the umbilical cord — became fetishes, and mankind’s first toy was a preserved umbilical cord. Geniuses were thought to be fetish personalities possessed by a wise spirit, and so chiefs, kings, priests, and prophets came to wield unbounded authority.
88.b10.t: Marked stones, volcanoes, comets, fire and water
The apple, apes, serpents, the cow
Unlucky Friday and thirteen; lucky four
Saliva, hair, fingernails, skulls, the umbilical cord
88.b12.p: Ghosts were thought to prefer to dwell in objects that had belonged to them in life, and this belief explains the efficacy of many relics. Belief in relics is an outgrowth of the ancient fetish cult; it is considered heathenish to believe in fetishes and magic but all right to accept relics and miracles. The earliest images were monuments to the illustrious dead, and idols were a refinement of fetishism.
88.b13.p: Moses tried to control fetish worship by adding the second commandment. It did much to retard art, but it lessened fetish worship. Eventually, however, words became fetishes — especially those regarded as God’s words — and the sacred books of many religions became prisons for man’s spiritual imagination. A fetishized doctrine hands man over to bigotry, fanaticism, and intolerance.
88.b15.p: Opening a sacred book at random to let a chance passage decide one’s life, or swearing an oath on a “holy book,” is a refined form of fetishism. Even so, it is real progress to move from fearing a chief’s fingernail trimmings to revering a collection of writings that reflects the winnowed moral wisdom of many centuries.
88.b16.t: Relics; pilgrimages to the tombs of great men
The adoration of a sacred book
A place where God’s spirit was thought to dwell
88.b18.p: Fetishism ran through all the primitive cults, from sacred stones through idolatry and nature worship to totemism. Totemism is a combination of social and religious observances. The totem was at once the symbol of the group and its god — the clan personified — and it eventually evolved into the flag, the national symbol of modern peoples.
88.b19.t: The medicine bag that must never touch the ground
The flag that must never touch the ground
The judgment of a fetish personality
88.b20.p: The book says that men have even made a fetish of democracy. One man’s opinion by itself is not thought worth much, but when many people’s same mediocre judgment is gathered up as “public opinion,” it is held to be the arbiter of justice and the standard of righteousness.
88.b22.p: Civilized man attacks the problems of a real environment with science; the savage tried to solve the problems of an imagined ghost environment with magic. Magic was the art of obtaining or coercing spirit co-operation by means of fetishes or more powerful spirits. Remarkably, the aims of magic and science are the same.
88.b23.t: 1. To secure insight into the future
88.b24.p: Mankind has progressed from magic to science not by meditation and reason but through long and painful experience. Man has been backing into the truth — beginning in error, progressing in error, and finally reaching the threshold of truth — and only with the scientific method has he faced forward. The fascination of early superstition was the mother of later scientific curiosity. The book records that, unable to grasp natural death, people would sometimes put ten innocent persons to death for one natural death. And because fear itself can kill, magic took an even firmer hold.
88.b26.p: Since anything connected with the body could become a fetish, the earliest magic centered on hair and nails. Burying excreta, covering spittle, and leaving no food remnants were done not for hygiene but for fear an enemy would use these things in magic. Effigies were believed to pass on to the real person whatever was done to them. Even the customs of a newer civilization — writing, printing, and pictures — were long regarded as evil magic.
88.b27.p: Names, too, mattered in magic. A name was a separate entity, as precious as the soul and the shadow, and it could even be pawned for a loan. One’s real name was never told to strangers, and so the everyday nickname arose.
88.b28.t: Pawning one’s name for a loan
Signing one’s name to a note
Buying a new name from the chief
88.b30.p: In magic, “medicine” meant mystery, not treatment. There was public magic, done by medicine men and priests for the good of the tribe, and private magic, used by witches and sorcerers to harm enemies; the idea of good and bad spirits led to the later beliefs in white and black magic. Some early incantations evolved into prayers, and prayer gradually displaced magic as the associate of sacrifice.
88.b31.p: Magic was the branch off the tree of evolutionary religion that eventually bore the fruit of a scientific age. But a world full of charms crushed personal ambition and initiative: a man whose field yielded more grain than his neighbor’s might be accused of enticing it away by magic, and it was dangerous to know very much. If modern methods of education should fail, there would be an almost immediate reversion to belief in magic.
88.b32.t: The science that grew from it
88.b33.p: Today Urantia is in the twilight zone of this intellectual evolution. Half the world is reaching eagerly for the light of truth and the facts of science, while the other half languishes in the arms of ancient superstition and thinly disguised magic.
88.b35.p: Paper 88 shows how far the old belief in spirits dwelling in objects has reached. Sacred stones and a chief’s fingernails have become relics and sacred books; totems and medicine bags have become flags and nations; spells and charms have become public opinion and titles — and they are still with us. Above all, when words become fetishes, scripture becomes a prison for the spiritual imagination, and doctrine hands people over to bigotry and intolerance. Yet the paper does not merely mock magic. The fascination of superstition was the mother of scientific curiosity, and magic was the cocoon in which science grew. Now our task is to leave that cocoon behind and move toward the light of truth.
88.b36.t: Stones, animals, even people — anything unusual became a spirit-filled fetish
Fetishes led to relics and sacred books, and doctrinal fetishes imprison man
The totem became the flag, and man fetishized even the state and public opinion
Magic and science share the same aims; mankind reached truth by way of error
Bits of the body and even names were feared as tools of magic
Magic, a branch of evolutionary religion, bore the fruit of science
88.b38.box: Magic was the cocoon of science; now man must shed the fear of fetishes and move toward the light of truth.
89.title: Sin, Sacrifice, and Atonement
89.b0.ask: “How did man move from appeasing the gods with bloody sacrifices to a forgiveness that is simply the renewal of loyalty?”
89.b2.p: In Paper 88 we saw how deeply fetishes, charms, and magic once ruled human life. Paper 89 now follows another idea: that man is in debt to the spirits. Primitive man regarded himself as owing something to the spirits and as standing in need of redemption. In time this notion grew into the doctrine of sin and salvation. The soul was thought to come into the world under forfeit — original sin — and it had to be ransomed.
89.b3.p: The savage believed that the spirits took satisfaction in the sight of human misery and suffering. At first he worried only about the wrongs he had done; later he worried also about the things he had left undone. The whole system of sacrifice grew up around these two ideas. Only an advanced civilization recognizes a God who is consistently even-tempered and kind.
89.b4.p: Taboo, renunciation, sacrifice, redemption — where does this long road finally lead? And how should we understand sin and forgiveness today?
89.b8.p: A taboo was a rule to avoid certain acts in order to escape bad luck and to keep from offending the spirit ghosts. At first taboos had nothing to do with religion, but once they gained the sanction of ghosts or spirits they became lawmakers and institution builders. The taboo was the source of ceremonial standards and the beginning of primitive self-control. For ages it was the only form of social regulation.
89.b9.p: The seven commands of Dalamatia and Eden, and the ten commandments of the Hebrews, were all taboos in the form of “⟦Q 89:2.1|140:4.7|140:5.9⟧thou shalt not.⟦/Q⟧” Yet these codes brought real freedom, for they took the place of thousands of older taboos, and they also promised a reward for obedience. Taboos were a heavy burden, but without them there would have been no civilized society to look back and criticize primitive man. The achievement of self-control lifted the race up the steps of civilization.
89.b10.t: Religious dietary rules, such as the taboo on pork
The seven commands and the ten commandments
89.b12.p: Religion began with magic and ghosts, passed through spirits and fetishes, and grew into taboos. Every primitive tribe had its tree of forbidden fruit, with its own “⟦Q 89:2.1|140:4.7|140:5.9⟧thou shalt not.⟦/Q⟧” Once men imagined good and bad spirits, and once taboo gained religious sanction, the idea of sin appeared. Sin was the breaking of a taboo, and death was its penalty. Only through the idea of sin could primitive man make sense of natural death.
89.b13.p: Sin was an act, not a thought; it was ritual, not rational. The traditions of Eden strengthened the belief that man had started out perfect and fallen by breaking a taboo. Primitive law turned vices into crimes, and religion turned them into sins. Hell was invented to explain why the wicked often prospered. Confession and forgiveness also appeared early, but they were only rites of absolution and of making a public show of one’s uncleanness.
89.b15.p: Renunciation was the next stage in the evolution of religion. Fasting and giving up the pleasures of the flesh became custom, and property came to be seen as a spiritual hindrance, so many sought poverty. Many of these forms were foolish, yet all of them taught the savage self-control. Self-denial and self-control were the two greatest social gains of early evolutionary religion.
89.b17.p: The continence cult tolerated marriage only as an evil lesser than fornication, and it entered Christian theology through the personal views of Paul. Paul himself admitted that he spoke “⟦Q 89:3.6⟧by permission and not by commandment,⟦/Q⟧” but the idea led to a war against marriage and the home and to celibate priesthoods. Self-control is a better way than extreme self-denial, and Jesus never taught such unreasonable views.
89.b19.p: Primitive man measured the worth of a sacrifice by the pain it cost him. The first sacrifices were pulling out hair or cutting the flesh. As civilization advanced, these were raised into rites of abstinence and fasting and into the doctrine of sanctification through sorrow. At first sacrifice was a levy imposed by the ancestor spirits; as the idea of original sin spread, it grew into the doctrine of atonement for racial guilt.
89.b20.t: Redemption — paying off what is owed
Putting something else in one’s place (a later development)
89.b21.p: Renunciation was the negative form of propitiation; sacrifice became the positive form. Propitiation came to include praise, glorification, and even flattery, and the remnants of these practices make up the modern forms of worship. In the end necessity drove men to eat the material part of their sacrifices — the gods, they said, had already enjoyed the soul of it — and this was justified as a sacred meal, a communion service in today’s terms.
89.b23.p: The book explains that early cannibalism, horrible as it seems to us, was part of the social and religious structure of primitive society. It arose from necessity and was kept alive by superstition and ignorance. Food was man’s greatest need, so men supposed it must be the spirits’ greatest need as well. Cannibalism was once almost universal among the evolving races, but originally the Andonites were not cannibals, nor were the Nodites and Adamites.
89.b24.p: The practice faded away slowly, through many stages. The parts that were eaten and the people who might eat them were gradually limited, and a taboo on cannibalism began in Dalamatia and slowly spread over the world. Finally, when human sacrifice became established, human flesh became the food of the gods alone, and men ate only a small ceremonial portion. Later still, animals came into general use as substitutes.
89.b25.t: It became a matter of group responsibility for an execution
It early became a ritual, though it did not always lessen
Organs thought to hold the soul, and the blood
It began in Dalamatia and spread
The flesh went to the gods; men ate only a small portion
89.b27.p: The book explains that human sacrifice was an indirect result of cannibalism as well as its cure. The practice was almost universal; no race was wholly free of it. The Chaldeans were among the first to offer animals instead of humans on ordinary occasions, and a Japanese emperor introduced clay images in place of living victims.
89.b28.p: The most tragic example is the story of Jephthah and his only daughter. Having made a foolish vow as the price of victory, Jephthah offered his daughter as a sacrifice, in spite of Moses’ strict rulings against human sacrifice. There were also foundation sacrifices, in which a person was buried beneath a new building; the custom of placing keepsakes in a cornerstone is a remnant of it. To the people of Abraham’s day, the story of Abraham and Isaac was not a strange idea.
89.b30.p: Moses tried to end human sacrifice through a substitute: redemption. Land, property, and children could all be redeemed by paying a fixed ransom. The groups that stopped sacrificing their first-born soon gained a great advantage over their neighbors. The book shows how human sacrifice was changed into many other forms.
89.b31.t: A ransom paid to the priests in place of a life
A rite to protect the first-born
If the child survived, the gods were thought to have intervened
Sending them away instead of killing them — the origin of colonization
The book records that this led to temple prostitution
89.b33.p: Redemption through sacrifice was itself a modification of human sacrifice, and next the offering of a part of the body took the place of a whole sacrifice. Men offered hair, nails, and blood. Circumcision too came not from hygiene but from partial sacrifice. Tattooing grew as an artistic development of the old practice of scarring the body.
89.b34.p: At last sacrifice became joined to the idea of the covenant. To think of the gods as making real agreements with man was a major step in the stabilization of religion. Man could not imagine trustworthy gods until he himself had become trustworthy and moral. Even so, the early sacrifices and prayers were not true worship; they were bargaining with the gods, petitions for a trade.
89.b37.p: Over long ages the rites of sacrifice advanced to higher and more symbolic levels and gave birth to the later sacramental services. The ideas of ransom, redemption, and covenant grew into the sacraments, and this evolution exerted a mighty socializing influence. The sacrament of bread and wine took the place of the flesh and blood of the older sacrifices, and the Christian sacrament grew out of the Passover ceremony.
89.b38.p: Paul built a new cult on “⟦Q 89:9.3⟧the blood of the everlasting covenant.⟦/Q⟧” He may have burdened Christianity with needless teachings about blood and sacrifice, but he did once and for all make an end of the doctrines of redemption through human or animal sacrifices. His compromise shows that even revelation must submit to the gradual control of evolution. Today salvation through blood has become, at least, figurative and symbolic.
89.b39.t: At first only the priests partook; later all shared the animal
Bread and wine — a figurative, symbolic salvation
89.b41.p: Ancient man could feel sure of God’s favor only through sacrifice. Modern man must find new ways of reaching the self-consciousness of salvation, for his spiritual needs are unchanged, while the old methods have been undone by intellectual progress. Sin must therefore be redefined as deliberate disloyalty to Deity. The feeling of guilt is only the awareness of having broken the mores; it is not necessarily sin.
89.b43.p: The capacity to feel guilt is not a stamp of shame on mankind; it marks man as a creature of potential greatness. Confession is a manful repudiation of disloyalty, and it is essential to spiritual growth. And divine forgiveness does not need to be begged for. It needs only to be received, as the awareness that the loyalty relationship has been restored.
89.b46.p: Paper 89 follows to the end the road mankind has walked in fearing sin and trying to pay its price. Taboo taught self-control. Renunciation left behind the wisdom of lowering one’s demands. Sacrifice climbed from cannibalism to human sacrifice, then to redemption and covenant, and finally to the symbolic sacrament. That road was dark and painful, but it was not in vain. Now this paper asks us to understand sin not as the breaking of a taboo but as conscious disloyalty to God. Then forgiveness is not something bought with a price. It is what a child who has returned to loyalty receives on realizing that the broken relationship has been mended.
89.b47.t: Taboo was the beginning of self-control and the first social regulation
Sin was at first not a thought but an act — breaking a taboo
The great gain was self-control that lowers the denominator of demands
Sacrifice, once measured by pain, grew into propitiation and atonement
Through many stages cannibalism became a taboo
Human sacrifice was almost universal and was slowly replaced
Moses’ redemption opened the way to end human sacrifice
The covenant took the place of luck, fear, and superstition
The cult of sacrifice grew into the symbolic cult of the sacrament
Sin is conscious disloyalty; forgiveness is the renewal of loyalty
89.b49.box: Sin is conscious disloyalty to God, and forgiveness is not earned by paying a price; it is received as the awareness of a restored relationship of loyalty.
90.title: Shamanism—Medicine Men and Priests
90.b0.ask: “The shamans and priests who claimed to stand between man and God — what did they block, and what did they leave behind for the human race?”
90.b2.p: In Paper 89 we saw how taboo, sacrifice, and atonement developed. Religious ritual advanced from avoidance, exorcism, coercion, and propitiation to sacrifice, atonement, and redemption, and its techniques passed through fetishes into magic and miracles. As the rituals grew more complex, they passed into the hands of medicine men, shamans, and priests.
90.b3.p: In the end, the spirit world came to be thought of as unresponsive to the ordinary man. Only special persons, people believed, could gain the ear of the gods, and so religion entered an indirect stage. Evolutionary religion is born of an all-powerful fear and at last comes to realize the all-powerful love of the Universal Father. But between that beginning and that fulfillment lie the long ages of the shamans, who presumed to stand between man and God as go-betweens.
90.b4.p: How did these intermediaries gain their power? How did they explain disease and death? And what did their rituals leave to the worship of today?
90.b8.p: The shaman was the head medicine man, the ceremonial fetish man, and the central personality of evolutionary religion. In many groups his authority went beyond that of the war chief — the first sign of the church beginning to dominate the state. Since anything abnormal was thought to be spirit-possessed, marked mental or physical oddities actually qualified a man to become a medicine man.
90.b9.p: Most shamans believed that they were possessed by spirits, but many were clever frauds. Drugs, sleight of hand, ventriloquism, and an accidental discovery of hypnotism all added to their air of mystery. Yet a shaman’s standing depended on visible results. If he failed and could not explain the failure, he was demoted or killed. So the honest shamans died out early, and only the shrewd actors survived.
90.b10.t: The shrewd, the clever, and the farsighted
90.b12.p: The ceremonies for calling up the spirits were as elaborate as the services of modern churches conducted in an ancient tongue. The shaman wielded great power of suggestion, though nearly always negative suggestion. His main work was not curing disease so much as knowing and controlling the hazards of life. Casting lots, signs and omens, primitive astrology, and the interpretation of dreams were all his tools. Once, the person on whom the lot fell had to die; today he only becomes “it” in a children’s game.
90.b13.t: Priests, seers, shamans, and medicine men — serving the tribe’s recognized gods
Sorcerers, magicians, witches, and wizards — dealing with unrecognized spirits
90.b14.p: Later, when witches came to be linked with the devil, the stage was set for much of the religious intolerance of fairly recent times. The shamans grew rich on their fees and became the original aristocracy, exempt from all tribal regulations, and they suppressed rivals by branding them witches. Still, in every age true prophets and teachers arose to denounce and expose shamanism. Primitive man feared the shaman but did not love him. Yet his respect for the shaman shows how high a value the race placed on wisdom.
90.b15.h: 3. The Shamanic Theory of Disease and Death
90.b16.p: Primitive man believed that he and his surroundings responded directly to the whims of ghosts, so it was natural for religion to be busy with material matters. Since all disease and death were seen as spirit happenings, it was inevitable that the shaman should also serve as doctor and surgeon. The primitive mind lacked facts, but it was still logical, and according to its level of understanding it produced five theories of affliction.
90.b17.t: Spirits lured the soul away — the sick were abandoned, which happened to act as quarantine
Obvious causes such as war or wild beasts were seen as natural events
The evil eye and the pointing bow — autopsies cut down accusations of witchcraft
Divine punishment for breaking a taboo or for racial guilt
First recognized by the Greeks — science breaking the chains of ignorance
90.b18.p: The book records that some tribes still pick out someone to kill whenever a nonviolent death occurs. The idea that sickness is a sign of divine anger is still widespread even among civilized peoples. But an understanding of aging and of contagion is slowly erasing the fear of ghosts and gods as the authors of suffering.
90.b21.p: The whole life of ancient man was preventive, and his religion was in large part a technique for preventing disease. He had boundless faith in his remedies, and that faith was itself a powerful medicine. In a society that feared and avoided the sick and left them to themselves, the appearance of priests and medicine men who set out to treat disease was a great humanitarian advance.
90.b22.t: Chanting, howling, laying on of hands, breathing on the patient, temple sleep
Opening the skull, setting fractures and dislocations, lancing boils, midwifery
Rubbing, cupping, bloodletting, sweating, foul-smelling medicines
Steam baths, hot springs, sunshine, hot stones and mud
Oil and wine, castor oil and opium, cocoa and quinine
90.b23.p: The Greeks were the first to treat the sick in truly rational ways, and both the Greeks and the Egyptians received their medical knowledge from the Euphrates valley. It is no accident that secret remedies lost their power once they became known. Secrecy has always been essential to fraud and superstition, but facts and truth welcome the light of understanding.
90.b25.p: To the savage, the essence of a ritual lay in performing it perfectly. Only a precise performance, he believed, could compel the spirits, so the shamans developed into priesthoods that carried out the rituals in minute detail. As a result, for tens of thousands of years endless ritual became an unbearable burden on every part of life. Ritual is the technique of making customs sacred; it creates and keeps alive the myths.
90.b26.t: Keepers of relics, temple caretakers, foretellers of events
The actual leaders of religious worship — later a hereditary caste
90.b27.p: The priests raised their authority by awing the people with an ancient tongue and mysterious magical passes. The great danger in all this is that ritual tends to become a substitute for religion. The priesthoods held back scientific and spiritual progress, but they did contribute to the stability of civilization.
90.b30.p: Paper 90 casts an honest light on the long age when intermediaries stood between man and God. The shamans made abnormality into inspiration, created mystery through trickery and suggestion, and piled up wealth and power. Their theories of disease were mostly wrong, and their endless rituals weighed heavily on life. Yet even then a humanitarian care for the sick took root, respect for wisdom grew, and true prophets and teachers again and again pointed the way. Fear was only the scaffolding for the idea of God, and evolution removes the scaffolding once it has served its purpose. At the end of that road, religion comes to realize, without any go-between, the all-powerful love of the Universal Father.
90.b31.t: The honest shamans disappeared; the shrewd actors survived
The shamans gained wealth and power, yet respect for them shows the value placed on wisdom
3. The Shamanic Theory of Disease and Death
From ghosts to natural causes — fear was the scaffolding for the idea of God
Priests who cared for the sick were a great humanitarian advance
The greatest danger is that ritual takes the place of religion
90.b33.box: Religion born of fear passes through the long age of intermediaries and at last arrives at the simple realization of the Universal Father’s all-powerful love.
91.title: The Evolution of Prayer
91.b0.ask: “How did prayer, which began as talking to oneself for good luck, become a conversation with the indwelling God?”
91.b2.p: In Paper 90 we saw the long age when shamans and priests stood between man and God. Paper 91 now turns to the channel of religion that runs through all those ages: prayer. Prayer grew out of nonreligious monologue and dialogue. When primitive man became self-conscious, other-consciousness followed, and this held two possibilities at once: social response and the recognition of God.
91.b3.p: The earliest prayers were not addressed to God. They were like saying to a friend before some big task, “⟦Q 91:0.2⟧Wish me luck.⟦/Q⟧” At first they were monologues, a kind of thinking out loud. When the ideas of ghosts and spirits arose, petition turned toward superhuman beings, and only when men became conscious of gods did they reach the level of real prayer.
91.b4.p: How, then, does prayer differ from magic? Does true prayer change God, or does it change us who pray?
91.b8.p: The work of early religion is to conserve and promote the growing social, moral, and spiritual values, and this is done chiefly through prayer. Without the protection of prayer, every holy day would soon slip back into a mere holiday. Religion and prayer were linked only with values that society approved, so anyone who wanted to reach a selfish or antisocial goal had to turn not to prayer but to magic and the sorcerer. In this way prayer early became a powerful force for moral progress.
91.b9.p: Primitive man also asked for material blessings such as food, rain, and game. This was a distortion of prayer, yet it spurred efforts to gain material ends through social and ethical conduct. Real prayer appears only when the agency of religious ministry is recognized as personal. The dangers of prayer lie in ignorance, superstition, crystallization, devitalization, materialism, and fanaticism.
91.b11.p: Prayer grew from an expressed wish into a technique for gaining the help of spirits, and then into the higher work of conserving everything of value. When men learned that the gods could not be coerced, prayer became petition. But the truest prayer is communion between man and his Maker.
91.b12.t: Active effort of the praying self
Manipulates reality without affecting the self
Turned material, it sinks into pseudo magic
As its aims rise, it nears the threshold of prayer
91.b13.p: The idea of sacrifice weakens the power of prayer, because men try to offer material things instead of offering a will dedicated to doing the will of God. Remove a personal God, and prayer becomes theology and philosophy; an impersonal God is fatal to the power of true prayer. Much prayer is a communion with one’s own subconscious self, but there is also a superconscious realm where contact is made with the indwelling Thought Adjuster. And prayer guards the personality against isolation.
91.b15.p: As children learn to speak, they think aloud, and before long they talk with imaginary companions, turning monologue into a pretended dialogue. Much adult thinking, too, is an inner conversation. Prayer grew in the same way. Recitations addressed to no one became talks with an alter ego, a second self, and when that alter ego was raised to divine dignity, prayer emerged as the channel of religion.
91.b16.t: One God — the embodiment of the highest ideals
The indwelling Adjuster — a real and divine alter ego
91.b17.p: Prayer is always a twofold experience: a psychological process joined with a spiritual technique. Enlightened prayer recognizes not only an external and personal God but also the inner Adjuster. Just as primitive man talked with a near-by alter ego, we can know that this idea has grown from a mere fiction into the truth of God dwelling in man through the Adjuster — so that we can talk with him face to face, as it were.
91.b19.p: A prayer that seeks a selfish advantage over one’s fellows cannot be ethical; it slips back into primitive pseudo magic. Prayer must never take the place of action, and every ethical prayer is a stimulus to action. We should pray fairly, not expecting God to love us more than our friends, our neighbors, or even our enemies.
91.b20.t: Self-centered — leads to disillusionment as science advances
Asking for forgiveness and the wisdom of self-control
Moves toward the level of true worship
91.b21.p: Even so, the spiritually advanced should be careful not to discourage the prayers of immature minds too quickly. Such petitions, too, lead to effort and labor toward their own answer.
91.b24.p: As the alter ego of prayer becomes more divine, man’s ideals rise from human to divine levels, his character improves, and his personality becomes deeply unified. Group prayer is very effective because its effects are highly socializing. Confession, repentance, and prayer have led individuals, cities, and nations to reform and to brave deeds.
91.b25.p: If you truly want to overcome the habit of criticizing a friend, the quickest and surest way is to pray for that person every day of your life. But the social effects of such prayers depend on two conditions. And those who can be conscious of God without symbols should not deny the gracious ministry of symbols to those who need forms and rituals.
91.b26.t: The person prayed for should know that he is being prayed for
The one who prays should come into close social contact with him
91.b28.p: Prayer cannot directly affect the physical environment unless it is linked with the will of the spiritual forces and the material supervisors. Prayer is not a technique for curing organic disease, but it has contributed much to healing mental, emotional, and nervous disorders, and it has made other treatments more effective. Even apart from its religious meaning, prayer is a sound psychological practice that reaches the reserve powers of human nature stored in the unconscious mind.
91.b30.p: We should pray as Jesus taught: honestly, unselfishly, fairly, and without doubting. And the power of prayer never depends on intellectual understanding, social standing, or cultural level. There is no more immediate way for anyone to reach the threshold of communion with the Creator than prayer.
91.b32.p: Mysticism deserves praise as a technique for cultivating the consciousness of God’s presence, but it is to be condemned when it leads to social isolation and fanaticism. Contact with the Adjuster occurs more often in unselfish, loving service to one’s fellows than in meditation. Jesus did take his apostles apart for a while to pray, but most of the time he had them serve the multitudes. The soul needs spiritual exercise as well as spiritual nourishment.
91.b33.p: Intense emotional experiences must not be mistaken for divine revelation. True spiritual ecstasy is usually joined with outward calm and emotional control. Whether such unusual experiences are genuine is tested by their fruits. The danger that too much private prayer will lead to isolation is corrected by group prayer and community worship.
91.b34.t: A more efficient and practical mental life
Greater love of truth, beauty, and goodness
Preserving social, moral, and spiritual values
91.b36.p: Primitive man prayed long before he had any clear idea of God. In distress he asked for help; in joy he poured out his delight. Prayer is not an evolution of magic; the two arose independently. True prayer is both moral and religious; magic is neither. Prayer may grow out of custom or fear, but true prayer is sincere and trusting communication between the spiritual nature of the creature and the spirit of the Creator.
91.b37.t: Seeking moral growth and spiritual strength
The joyful expression of a liberated son
91.b38.p: Even when the air currents are rising, no bird can soar unless it spreads its wings; prayer is the technique of riding the ascending spiritual currents of the universe. God answers prayer with a larger revelation of truth, a deeper appreciation of beauty, and a higher concept of goodness. Words are only a channel; God answers the soul’s attitude, not the words.
91.b41.p: To pray effectively, we must keep in mind the laws of prevailing petitions. These laws show that prayer is not a refuge for the lazy. It is offered by one who has faced his problems bravely, has done all he can, and chooses and does the will of God.
91.b42.t: Facing the problems of reality sincerely and bravely
Honestly using up every possibility of human adjustment
Yielding every wish and longing to the transforming embrace of spiritual growth
Wholeheartedly choosing the divine will, putting an end to indecision
Devoting oneself to actually doing the Father’s will
Asking for divine wisdom to solve the problems met in the ascent
91.b44.p: Paper 91 shows the path of prayer as if it were the growth of a single person. Talking to oneself for luck became a conversation with an imaginary companion; that alter ego rose through ghosts and gods to the one God, and at last reached the truth of the Adjuster who dwells within us. Prayer falls into magic when it seeks things and tries to change God, but it lifts up the personality when it seeks values and tries to change oneself. So prayer is not a substitute for action but its guide, not an escape into isolation but a channel into loving service. God answers not our words but the attitude of the soul.
91.b45.t: From the beginning prayer was a force for preserving social and moral values
Prayer moves the self; magic tries to manipulate reality without it
The fictional alter ego grew into the truth of the indwelling Adjuster
Prayer changes not God but the one who prays
Group prayer and intercession change people and communities
Face your problems bravely, and ask for wisdom and strength
True religious experience is tested by its fruits and its service
Ask for values, not things; for growth, not gratification
Courage, diligence, dedication, and living faith are the conditions of prayer
91.b47.box: True prayer is not a bargain to change God but a path of growth, in which we talk with the indwelling God and bring ourselves into line with his will.
92.title: The Later Evolution of Religion
92.b0.ask: “How does man’s religion, born of fear, meet revelation and grow until it worships a God of love?”
92.b2.p: In Paper 91 we saw how prayer, which began as an incantation, grew into communion with God. Paper 92 now looks back over the larger vessel that holds prayer — religion as a whole — and the road it has traveled.
92.b3.p: The book tells us that man had a religion of natural origin long before he received any systematic revelation. That religion arose slowly through three divine ministries, and later the Thought Adjusters, the seraphim, and the Spirit of Truth were added to speed its growth.
92.b4.p: What, then, did evolutionary religion, which began in fear, do well and do badly? How does revelation lift it up? And how should we look at religion today?
92.b8.t: Influences that gave rise to religion
Awakens man’s primitive instinct toward Deity
Leads adoration to higher expression and a wider concept of Deity
The first supermind bestowal, which brings belief in and experience of survival
92.b9.p: Religion began with the fear of ghosts, moved from trying to coerce the spirits to trying to appease them. Fetishes became totems and tribal gods; magic formulas became prayers; circumcision, once a sacrifice, became a sanitary practice. Mankind went from nature worship through ghost worship to fetishism, and has now entered a stage where it can understand true religion.
92.b10.p: Fear has always been the basic stimulus of religion. As civilization grows, fear is softened into awe and reverence, and then into remorse and repentance. One Asiatic people taught that “⟦Q 92:1.5⟧God is a great fear,⟦/Q⟧” but Jesus proclaimed that “⟦Q 92:1.5|1:3.8|2:5.1⟧God is love.⟦/Q⟧” The whole road of religion lies between those two sayings.
92.b12.p: Religion is the most rigid of all human institutions, yet it slowly adjusts itself to a changing society. Religion treats old things as sacred. That is why stone implements remained on the altars long into the bronze and iron ages, and why the most primitive foods were used in the sacraments. Old scriptures still hold passages that seem awkward today because men feared to erase what their ancestors held holy.
92.b13.p: The book says it is foolish to hurry the growth of religion too fast. A people can absorb a new religion only as far as it fits their stage of evolution; in fact, the morality of a race determines the form of its religion. The book also makes it plain that conscience is not a divine voice speaking to the soul, but only the sum of the moral content of the mores of the time.
92.b16.p: Studying religion is like digging through social layers that hold the fossils of past ages. Cults arose not to seek truth but to spread creeds, and religion has often been tainted by the delusion of being a chosen people. Evolutionary religion has no built-in way of correcting itself, as science does; it is corrected only by the pressure of the mores and the light of epochal revelation.
92.b17.p: The book judges evolutionary religion to have been man’s most expensive but incomparably effective institution. Religion has done much harm, yet without it there would have been no lasting morality and no civilization worth the name.
92.b18.t: Gave birth to sculpture, architecture, poetry, music, drama, and the dance
Accumulation of capital, discipline and self-control, social continuity
Hindered industry and wasted labor and capital
The whip of evolution, driving mankind toward reason and wisdom
92.b19.p: This sacred heritage, then, should not be thrown away. It must be refined again and again by the censorship of revealed religion and in the fiery furnace of genuine science.
92.b21.p: Revelation always keeps in touch with evolution, giving more light little by little, as much as man can receive. Revealed religion is always marked by belief in a Deity of final values and by the idea that personality survives death. If evolutionary religion is a roundabout path in search of truth, revealed religion is that truth itself.
92.b22.p: There have been many religious revelations, but only five of epochal significance.
92.b23.t: The one hundred members of the Prince’s staff proclaimed the First Source and Center
Adam and Eve again presented the concept of the Father of all
God’s favor is won by trust and faith
God as the Universal Father — love and service
The most recent revelation, prepared by many beings together
92.b24.p: The book is frank about itself as well. Until the Universal Father is reached, no revelation can be complete; all celestial ministry is partial and temporary.
92.b26.p: Evolutionary religion pictures God in the image of man; revealed religion teaches that man is a son of God. Man’s idea of God is a blend of the ideas of the evolutionary cults, the lofty ideals of revelation, and the personal views of great leaders.
92.b27.p: People tend to revere the leader more than the teaching. There is an instinct to look for help from above, and since Urantia lost its superhuman leaders, men try to fill that loss by wrapping human leaders in legends of miracles. Even so, these teachers were the fulcrums on which the levers of revealed truth rested. The leaders since Adam can be grouped into seven eras.
92.b28.t: The Sethite priests under Amosad preserved the concept of the Trinity
Proclaimed that faith is the way to God’s favor
Amenemope, Ikhnaton, and Moses, who taught one God
Gautama, Confucius, Lao-tse, Zoroaster, and the Jainist teachers
Jesus, and with him Paul and Philo
The division of Western Christianity, and Nanak with the Sikh religion
92.b29.p: The book says that teachers will yet come who will proclaim the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of all creatures. It hopes that they will foster a brotherhood of spiritual worship rather than raise higher the walls between religions.
92.b31.p: The book explains that the peoples of the twentieth century stood at very different stages of religious evolution. Some groups were still in the stage of ghost fear or fetishes, while others had long believed in one God and in immortality. In this age evolutionary and revelatory religion grew side by side and blended together, appearing as eleven great religions.
92.b32.t: The link between evolutionary and revealed religion
Spread widely by adapting to the mores of many peoples
The two streams followed by the Chinese
Faith in the triumph of light over darkness
One of the four religions of India
Formulated by Philo, Peter, and Paul, and thoroughly Occidentalized
Became a monotheistic faith under Jewish and Christian influence
The most recent religion to appear
92.b33.p: The book points to the way Islam stumbled over the doctrine of the Trinity to show how hard it always is for an evolving mind suddenly to accept an advanced revelation. It also notes that ancestor worship has revived in the West as a hero-worshiping nationalism, and that national religion is a return to the ancient worship of the state.
92.b35.p: Religion can never become a scientific fact, and a new religion cannot be invented. Religions only evolve or are revealed, and the old does not vanish but blends with the new. So no group should regard its own creed as the only truth. Every religion holds truth, and it is far better to borrow the best in a neighbor’s living faith than to condemn the worst in its superstitions.
92.b37.p: True religion is the devotion of the self to the highest values, a living experience of loving loyalty. The quality of a religion can be measured in four ways.
92.b38.t: The degree of dedication to divine values
Realizing sonship with God and endless universe citizenship
92.b39.p: A child’s religious experience depends greatly on whether fear or love ruled his relationship with his parents. The book regrets that those who revere the risen Christ have overlooked the man Joshua ben Joseph, the brave hero. Modern man must make more readjustments of values in one generation than were made in the past two thousand years, and in this task true religion must be the lasting foundation and the guiding star of civilization.
92.b41.p: Paper 92 neither condemns religion as a shameful past nor defends it blindly. Evolutionary religion, born of fear, wasted much and blocked much, yet it preserved civilization and morality and made room for revelation. Revelation has added light as fast as man could receive it, and that light has spread through the lives of great leaders. Now the many religions can become one — not in creed but in true worship of the Father. From “⟦Q 92:1.5⟧God is a great fear⟦/Q⟧” to “⟦Q 92:1.5|1:3.8|2:5.1⟧God is love,⟦/Q⟧” the end of that long journey is a brotherhood that borrows the best from one another.
92.b42.t: Religion begins in fear and grows toward the God of love
Religion clings to the old, and conscience is not a divine voice
Most expensive yet most effective, it must be refined again and again
Five epochal revelations have lifted evolutionary religion
The teachers of seven religious eras became fulcrums for truth
Evolution and revelation blended into the religions of today
All religions can be one in true worship
92.b44.box: Religion grows from fear to love, and all religions can become one in true worship of the Father.
93.title: Machiventa Melchizedek
93.b0.ask: “In an age when the light of truth was dying out, how did a Melchizedek who became a man prepare the way for Jesus?”
93.b2.p: In Paper 92 we saw that the third of the five epochal revelations came through Melchizedek of Salem. Paper 93 now tells the story of that revelation’s central figure, Machiventa Melchizedek.
93.b3.p: The Melchizedeks are known as the emergency Sons, who step forward whenever an unusual problem arises; they are a rare order able to work even on the level of physical personality. Twelve Melchizedeks took charge of this world after the Caligastia secession, and after the default of Adam and Eve they returned and remained as planetary receivers until Jesus became the nominal Planetary Prince.
93.b4.p: When even heavenly help seemed to be withheld, why did one Melchizedek take on a human body? And how was the covenant of faith he left behind carried forward — and then forgotten?
93.b8.p: For thousands of years after the Adamic mission failed, revealed truth was in danger of vanishing. Mankind went forward intellectually but slipped back spiritually, and by about 3000 B.C. the concept of God had grown very dim. The twelve receivers appealed to Edentia and to Father Melchizedek for help, but they were told only to keep the truth alive by means of their own choosing until a bestowal Son should come.
93.b9.p: Then one of the twelve, Machiventa, volunteered to do what had been done only six times in the whole history of Nebadon: to personalize on earth as a temporary man of the realm, bestowing himself as an emergency Son. With the permission of Salvington, he was materialized near the place later called Salem, with the help of the Life Carriers and other celestial personalities.
93.b11.p: Machiventa first appeared, without any display, 1,973 years before the birth of Jesus, in the tent of Amdon, a Chaldean herder. He ate with the shepherd and began to teach him the reality of God beneath the stars; a few years later he became the center of the Salem community. On his breastplate he wore three concentric circles, the symbol of the Paradise Trinity.
93.b12.t: Ninety-four years; he left before his body wore out
A special body like those of the Prince’s staff, without human life plasm
He never married and could leave no offspring
The very Adjuster who would later indwell Jesus
Full contact only with his eleven fellow receivers
93.b13.p: Above all, the Adjuster who indwelt him gained experience through this mission, which prepared him to work in the mind of Michael when Michael later came in human flesh. This is the only Thought Adjuster who has ever functioned in two minds on Urantia.
93.b15.p: Melchizedek founded schools at Salem, patterned on the old Sethite system of education. He taught one universal Deity, yet he allowed people to link his teaching with the Most Highs of Edentia. Most took the three circles to mean the three kingdoms of men, angels, and God; very few understood that they stood for the infinity, eternity, and universality of the Trinity.
93.b16.p: He taught each pupil as much as he could receive. To his brilliant pupil Nordan he imparted even the truths of the superuniverse and Havona, and the family of Katro kept his teachings until the days of Moses. He placed all his teaching under the doctrine of one God, a divine Father, and he foretold that another Son of God would one day be born of a woman. Michael came and confirmed everything that Melchizedek had taught about the Father.
93.b18.p: The worship at Salem was very simple. Everyone who signed the roll repeated and accepted three beliefs.
93.b19.t: El Elyon, the only Universal Father and Creator of all
God’s favor is given not for sacrifices but for faith
Keep the commandments and tell the good news to all
93.b20.p: The seven commandments were patterned on the supreme law of ancient Dalamatia and on the commandments of Eden.
93.b21.t: Serving any God but the Most High Creator
Doubting that faith is the only requirement for eternal salvation
Showing disrespect for parents and elders
93.b22.p: People simply could not grasp the idea that favor was received freely, by faith. Melchizedek gave them the sacrament of bread and wine in place of sacrifices, but the custom of sacrifice never died out, not even with Abraham. He had not come to change the mores or the customs. He came to keep alive the truth of one God and to prepare for the bestowal of a Paradise Son.
93.b24.p: It may be a mistake to speak of a chosen people, but it is not a mistake to call Abraham a chosen individual. Salem was chosen because Palestine was then the center of trade, travel, and civilization, and because contact could be made with the gifted children of Terah. Abraham and his nephew Lot came to Salem at Melchizedek’s invitation.
93.b25.p: But Abraham cherished ambitions to be a king. He wanted to spread the truth of Salem by subduing the neighboring tribes with the sword, and Melchizedek, who kept the peace, had a hard time restraining him. They parted on friendly terms, and Abraham set up a military capital at Hebron. When Lot’s goods were plundered, Abraham won the battle of Siddim and gave a tenth of the spoils to Salem.
93.b27.p: Dreaming of conquering Canaan, and troubled that he had no son to follow him, Abraham came again to Melchizedek. In this meeting he gave up worldly conquest and accepted the spiritual idea of the kingdom of heaven. Melchizedek pointed to the stars of heaven and promised that his seed would be as many; Abraham believed, and it was counted to him as righteousness.
93.b29.p: This good news — that salvation comes not by works but by faith — was too advanced, and in the end the people went back to the older system of bloody sacrifices. When Isaac was born as promised, Abraham put the covenant in writing and changed his name from Abram to Abraham. Once the reconciliation was complete, he became a leader at Salem and greatly improved its schools, missions, and tithing system.
93.b31.p: The missionaries trained by Melchizedek went out to Egypt, Mesopotamia, and Asia Minor, and on to Europe, the British Isles, Iceland, China, and even Japan. The lives of these men and women form one of the heroic chapters in human history.
93.b32.p: But the task was too great. Outside Palestine, the idea of one God never won the lasting loyalty of a whole tribe or race, and the gospel of Salem was almost buried under older cults such as the Great Mother and sun worship. In an age without printing, new truth was easily forgotten, and a new revelation was always contaminated by the older beliefs.
93.b34.p: Shortly after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Machiventa decided to end his bestowal. The chief reason was that people had begun to regard him as a demigod and to revere him with superstitious fear. He also judged that if he left while Abraham was still alive, the truth of one God would become firmly rooted in the minds of his followers. One night he said good night to his companions and went into his tent, and in the morning he was not there.
93.b36.p: The disappearance of Melchizedek was a lifelong sorrow to Abraham. For a while he was gripped by fear and even concealed his identity at Gerar, but he soon became again the spiritual leader of Palestine, and he died confident in the faith he had learned from Melchizedek. After five hundred years many regarded the story of Melchizedek as a myth, and Joseph, because of that belief, was called a dreamer by his brothers.
93.b37.p: The book explains that what the Old Testament records as conversations between Abraham and God were really conferences between Abraham and Melchizedek. It also says that the scribes of the Babylonian captivity, in their national pride, edited the records to exalt Abraham and almost erased the age of Melchizedek. As a result the teaching about the promised bestowal Son was lost too, and when Michael came, very few recognized him. Only one writer, the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, understood Melchizedek’s mission.
93.b39.p: On the third day after his disappearance from Salem, Machiventa reappeared among his eleven fellows and took up again his career as a planetary receiver. His arrival and his departure were not attended by any resurrection roll call or the end of a dispensation. For the next nineteen centuries he worked with the prophets to keep alive the truth of Salem.
93.b40.t: One of the four and twenty directors of Urantia on Jerusem
Personal ambassador of the Creator Son, Vicegerent Planetary Prince
Less than a thousand years ago
Resident governor general, invisibly present for one hundred years
Thought likely destined to take the place of Caligastia
93.b41.p: The book says that one day we may see Machiventa, Adam and Eve, Christ Michael, and a Magisterial Son or Trinity Teacher Sons all present on Urantia at once. That is why Urantia is one of the most interesting spheres in all Nebadon. Machiventa is among the most unique personalities ever connected with this world’s history, and he may yet play an important role in its future.
93.b43.p: Paper 93 is the story of a Melchizedek who became a man to keep a lamp burning when the light of truth was going out. Instead of sweeping reforms, he left a simple covenant: God’s favor is received not by works but by faith. People could not bear that gospel and went back to sacrifices, and later records even blurred his name. Yet his teaching passed on through Abraham and Moses and prepared the way for Jesus. And he has not left this planet. As Vicegerent Planetary Prince, representing Michael, he still shares in the future of Urantia.
93.b44.t: As truth faded, one receiver volunteered to become a man
He lived ninety-four years in a special body and prepared Jesus’ Adjuster
He placed all his teaching under one God, the divine Father
A simple creed and seven commandments: favor comes by faith, not sacrifice
Abraham, who dreamed of conquest, was chosen as Melchizedek’s pupil
A covenant in which God does everything and man only believes
They went to far lands, but the gospel was buried under old cults
To prevent demigod worship, he left quietly one night
As the records were blurred, the teaching about the bestowal Son was lost
He now serves this world as Vicegerent Planetary Prince, representing Michael
93.b46.box: Through Melchizedek, the covenant of faith — God does everything, and man only believes — was left on earth and prepared the way for Jesus.
